The automotive HPDC aluminum alloys will normally go through an e-coating process to deposit paint on the surface before joining. The e-coating involves heating to temperatures which will only cause aging which leads to fine precipitation from a supersaturated matrix phase, such as the Al-dendrite. The e-coating process will generally not cause meso-scale microstructural change. 6 (a) 200x Edge (b) 200x Center (c) 500x Edge (d) 500x Center Fig. 1 the typical microstructures of the HPDC aural-5 alloy plate with a thickness of 2.85 mm near the edge (a) and (b) in the center with 200x magnification; near the edge (c) and in the center (d) with 500x magnification. The dark region represents pores in the microstructure. 4.2 Tension, 3-point bending and clinch Test Specimen Manufacturing Tension, 3-point bending has been performed for the both the as-cast and e-coated Aural-5 alloy and the clinch test has been performed on the e-coated alloy. 4.2.1 Tension test The engineering stress-strain curves of the tensile tests for the as-cast and e-coated aural-5 alloys are as shown in Fig. 2. This figure shows that the as-cast alloy has lower yield stress (~90 MPa), but elongations ranges from 3.8% to 8.4%. The e-coated alloy has a yield stress of ~130 MPa, with the elongations range from 3.5% to 5.8%. In general conclusion, the e-coated alloy has higher strength, but relatively lower ductility than the as-cast alloy. 7 300 250 200 150 100 50 0 0 2 4 6 8 Fig. 2. The tensile stress-strain curves pf the As-Cast and E-Coated aural-5 HPDC alloy of 2.85mm thickness. 4.2.2 3-P bending test The geometry of the 3-point bending test is as shown in Fig. 3. During the test, the sharp punch plate with a tip radius of 0.2 mm is pushing upwards against the rollers which are kept stationary. The gap between the two rollers is the sum of two times the aural-5 plate thickness and the punch blade thickness. The load (F)-displacement (d) curve of two As-Cast alloy samples and two E-coated samples are as shown in Fig. 4. As can be seen from this figure, the load for the E-coated alloy is about 25% higher than that of as-cast alloy when d is the same. This is consistent with the stress-strain curves of the two alloys, where the E-coated alloy show higher engineering stresses than the as-cast alloy, when the engineering strains are the same. The higher strength of the E-coated alloy should be due to the fine precipitation during the E-coating heating process.
